newsitem.title: INDIA: Key state poll may change India ruling alliance.
newsitem.headline: Key state poll may change India ruling alliance.

text.p: India's fractious ruling alliance, pushed together by the rise of a Hindu nationalist opposition, could seek new partnerships after this week's local polls in the country's most populous state, politicians said.

The assembly elections in Uttar Pradesh state, bordering Nepal and Tibet, could decide if Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front government would continue to get support from the Congress Party, they told Reuters during the weekend.

Deve Gowda, whose four-month-old United Front coalition depends on the Congress party to beat off an unceasing challenge in parliament from the rightist Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), wants the Congress to eventually join his government.

On the other hand, closer ties between the United Front and the Congress party of former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao could force Deve Gowda's leftist allies to distance themselves from his government, senior communist leaders said.
But the state polls in Uttar Pradesh ending this week have pitted Deve Gowda's party against a coalition of the Congress and the low caste Hindu Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP).
Opinion polls say that the elections may produce a hung assembly, but they give the BJP an outside chance to form a government on its own.
The Congress has asked Deve Gowda to support a Congress-BSP alliance after the Uttar Pradesh polls to thwart the BJP in the state of 140 million, more populous than Japan or Pakistan.

"We have supported the Deve Gowda government in Delhi. It is now their turn to support us in Uttar Pradesh," Congress' state party spokesman, Ramesh Dixit, told Reuters. "If they don't, we will reconsider our support (to Deve Gowda's government)."

Politicians said such a move by Deve Gowda would need to be cleared by his defence minister, Mulayam Singh Yadav, a former socialist chief minister of Uttar Pradesh whose Samajawadi Party disapproves of any ties with the BSP.
BSP leader Mayawati (eds; one name) fell out with Yadav after a short-lived alliance in 1993 when they together defeated the BJP in the Uttar Pradesh assembly polls.

But Mayawati last year ditched Yadav's government when she briefly became chief minister with the BJP's backing. The BJP soon withdrew its support to her BSP government, forcing New Delhi to clamp direct rule on Uttar Pradesh.
Politicians said both Yadav and Deve Gowda's communist allies could come out weakened from the Uttar Pradesh polls.

"It is quite clear that if he is forced to choose, Deve Gowda would prefer to go with the Congress rather than seek our support," a senior state politician of the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPM) told Reuters.

"Indian communists see the Congress as their main foe in the leftist bastions of West Bengal and Kerala states," a Congress politician said. "The CPM-led ruling alliances in the two states are opposed to any role for the Congress in Deve Gowda's government."

Uttar Pradesh, which sends 85 lawmakers to parliament, the largest contingent from any state, became the BJP's main base following its recent campaign to build a Hindu temple at the site of a 16th century mosque.
